title: Unit 1 · What changes can inventions bring to our lives?
text: Fu Xing: What do you think is the most useful invention of all time, Peter? Peter: It has to be the radio. Fu Xing: The radio? Why? Peter: Before the radio was invented, information travelled very slowly. The world was made much smaller by the radio. Suddenly, news could be spread around the world in seconds. Fu Xing: Right. Who was the inventor? Peter: An Italian inventor called Guglielmo Marconi. He developed the idea in the 1890s. In 1901, a radio message was sent across the Atlantic Ocean for the first time. Fu Xing: Wow! That was quite a distance at that time. Peter: Yeah. And because of the radio, some other important inventions were developed as well. Fu Xing: Like the television? Peter: That's right. It also had a big effect on music. The radio made it much easier for people to enjoy music from artists around the world.

title: Unit 1 · How do we turn ideas into reality?
text:
Can you imagine a world without books, newspapers, or magazines? All of these things depend on one invention—papermaking. It, more than any other invention, was responsible for the rapid spread of information that shaped our modern world.

In ancient China, many different materials were used to write on, such as animal bones, bronze ware, stones, wood, bamboo, and even silk. In the Western Han Dynasty, there was also a very early form of paper made from jute—a fibre that comes from plants. However, all of these materials were either difficult to use and store, or very expensive.

As the head officer of the palace workshop for the emperor in the Eastern Han Dynasty, Cai Lun became interested in trying to solve the problem. Different methods for creating something to write on were tried, but none were ideal. In his time, some kinds of bark—the outer part of trees—were used to make clothes. From past experiences, Cai Lun got the idea that bark, certain plants, and old clothes could be used to make a special material suitable to write on.

In the first step of Cai Lun's experiment, all the ingredients were mixed and boiled in water. Then, this material was beaten, cut up, and mixed with water again. Next, the liquid was poured over a bamboo screen, leaving just the fibre. Finally, this fibre was dried and pressed to form paper. To everyone's surprise, this paper was soft, light, easy to make and use, and most importantly, cheap. In 105 CE, Cai Lun showed his creation to the emperor. The emperor was very pleased and praised Cai Lun for his great work.

of Chinese culture, but also changed civilizations around the world. It first spread to China's neighbouring countries and finally reached Europe through Arab countries in the 12th century. When the use of paper and printing came together in later centuries, it led to a rapid increase in the number of books. This resulted in a new birth of knowledge, creating the world we have today.

The invention of the plane has greatly changed the world. However, it seems that its inventors, Orville Wright and Wilbur Wright, were not looking to change the world at all. Rather, they just wanted to fly like birds.

To solve the problem of heavier-than-air flight, the Wright brothers began working with gliders. There were two main challenges. The first was how to get the glider into the air. The second was how to control it once it was flying. For both problems, they found their solutions by looking at how birds flew. After they solved these problems, they added an engine to the glider. Then, in December 1903, the world's first plane flights were made.

The invention of the plane has made our travels around the world much easier and faster. Journeys that once took days, weeks, or even months, can now be made in only a few hours. As a result, communication among people in different countries is now much easier, and the world has become a much smaller place.

title: Unit 1 · High-speed Rail
text:
While high-speed rail was not invented in China, the country has developed this technology to a new level. To increase the quality of high-speed railways and high-speed trains, China has overcome a lot of difficulties caused by technology, landforms, and bad weather conditions. At the end of 2025, China had a total railway length of about 165,000 kilometres, including 50,400 kilometres of high-speed railways. China's high-speed rail network is the longest and fastest in operation in the world. It is leading the world now and has become a model of "China Speed".

China's high-speed rail system has won praise at home and abroad. Foreign visitors to China are deeply impressed by the high-speed rail service, finding it timely, quiet, comfortable, and convenient. For instance, a video shared by a Swedish visitor shows a coin standing steadily for eight minutes without falling in a high-speed train travelling at 300 kilometres per hour. There are countless similar videos on the internet. Among different high-speed trains, Fuxing bullet trains are the most advanced. They are completely designed and produced by China. Fuxing bullet trains offer Wi-Fi networks and have a lot of legroom. It is not surprising that high-speed trains have become the first choice for travellers in China.

title: Unit 1 · Why do we explore space?
text:
Our question today is: Why do we explore space? Let's talk to space scientist Dr Yang. Welcome, Dr Yang! Dr Yang: Thank you very much. Well, there are three good reasons to explore space. First, to improve our knowledge of Earth and its place in the universe. Could you explain that a bit more? Dr Yang: Sure. The study of other planets helps us better understand Earth's geology, history, and relationship with other planets. Oh, right. Dr Yang: Second, technology developed for space can benefit us here on Earth. Could you give our listeners an example? Dr Yang: Of course. Some satellites, for example, help us deal with problems caused by climate change. Yes, that's very useful. And the third reason? Dr Yang: Well, at some point in the far future, we may find new resources in outer space. It might sound crazy, but our Earth may run out of resources. In that case, a new home for us human beings will be needed. Wow, interesting! Maybe Mars will be turned into our new home in the future.

It is believed that our understanding of the moon and the universe will be greatly improved.

title: Unit 1 · How far can we go into space?
text:
Before you read, decide what kind of text it is. Is it a sci-fi story, popular science article, news report, or something else?

Since the beginning of human history, people have looked up at the stars and wondered what they were like. Many ancient cultures believed that these points of light were from gods or other mysterious worlds. However, as technology and science developed, we learnt the truth about stars. They are real places like our own sun, and they are farther away than anyone imagined. This raises the question: Can we visit the stars one day?

The man-made object which has travelled farthest from Earth is Voyager 1. This spacecraft was launched in 1977. In case Voyager 1 is found by alien life, a special record with sounds and pictures from Earth is carried on board. It shows who we are and where we are from. By 2025, Voyager 1 was over 25 billion kilometres from Earth, but that is still a long way from Earth's second-closest star, Proxima Centauri. That star is 4.2 light years away—about 40 trillion kilometres!

The challenge of visiting the stars gets even bigger for space flights with humans. The farthest that any human has travelled in space is only about 400,000 kilometres, to the far side of the moon. Time is a big problem. At present, even a journey to the planet Mars will take around six to nine months. What will the astro- nauts eat and drink during this period? And how about their health and safety? These problems grow when we talk about visiting another star. It might take hundreds of thousands of years to get there!

Scientists, however, believe that visiting the stars is not a completely wild dream. One idea is to have the astronauts sleep during their journey, like some animals do in winter. Another is to develop much faster spacecraft.

While this is not possible right now, with nations and scientists cooperating with one another, there is hope that the necessary technology will be developed. Humans have photographed other galaxies, set foot on the moon, and even successfully landed rovers on Mars. It seems likely that one day we will reach the stars.

My space dream is that one day a research station will be built on the moon. I believe there are quite a few benefits.

First, it will be a good place for scientists to cooperate and do space research together. New technologies can be developed, tested, and operated there. These technologies can then be used to help build stations on Mars and other planets.

Second, more resources will be found. I think the moon may have some special kind of energy resource that can be useful to Earth. It will just take time for scientists to find it.

Third, people may live and work there. Tourists will also be able to visit. I want to be one of the first visitors. I hope that one day we humans can spend holidays in space and explore the universe.

Humans have achieved many things that were once only dreams. I hope the research station on the moon will be built in the near future, and I hope it will happen during my lifetime.

build a research station on the moon send a spacecraft to the nearest star system search for life in the solar system build a satellite to collect the sun's energy and send it to Earth ...

title: Unit 1 · Space Lectures
text:
On 20 June 2013, the first space lecture was given to more than 60 million primary and middle school students in China. It was given by astronaut Wang Yaping with the help of her crewmates. The lecture lasted about 50 minutes. China became the second country to offer a lesson to schoolchildren directly from space.

Eight years after the first space lecture, on 9 December 2021, the crewmates in China's Tiangong space station offered another lecture. It was about how astronauts work and live in the station and how objects move in space. During this lecture, students were able to communicate with the astronauts in real time.

The third lecture took place on 23 March 2022. During the lesson, the astronauts performed four experiments to show physical phenomena that are only possible in a weightless environment.

to do similar experiments along with them, allowing students to observe the differences between space and Earth and discover the joy of scientific exploration.

More space lectures are planned for the future. Students of all ages will have opportunities to observe experiments and interact with astronauts. China's space station will be fully made use of to encourage young people to learn about space science.

title: Unit 1 · What is the power of music?
text:
When the great composer Robert Schumann first heard a work which was written by young Chopin, he said, "Hats off, gentlemen! A genius!"

Frédéric Chopin (1810–1849) is considered one of the greatest musicians in history. During his short lifetime, he was celebrated as one of the world's greatest pianists— even though he only gave around 30 concerts! He was also a gifted composer who left behind more than 200 musical works.

Chopin was born in a village in Poland. He didn't attend music school until he was 16, but soon outdid his teachers. His parents sent him to Vienna in 1829 to widen his musical experience. By 1832, he had made his way to Paris, the city that he would call home for the rest of his life.

Chopin was not only a great pianist, but also a respected piano teacher. He often told his students, "Put all your soul into it! Play the way you feel!" This is advice that is still followed by musicians today.

Polish folk music was a kind of music that some people looked down on at the time—it was seen as too simple and common. But it became an important characteristic of Chopin's music. His use of Polish folk music caused people to see it as a valuable art form.

His music also helped build a nation which was divided up by other countries. By using Polish folk music, Chopin seemed to be saying to the world, "We are our own country with our own culture! We are our own people!" Chopin's music encouraged his people and helped them keep going through years of difficulty. Today, the Polish people proudly think of Poland as the country of Chopin.

When Chopin died from ill health at 39, thousands of people travelled from faraway countries to attend his funeral. Today, people around the world still listen to his moving and often sad music. It is studied in music schools, played by pianists, heard in films and on TV, and loved by listeners young and old.

The present that changed my life was the guitar my father bought me for my eighth birthday. I spent the next several months learning to play the guitar. I often sat next to my father while he showed me how to play a song. Then I went to my room and practised until my fingers hurt. I had a lot of trouble at first. But gradually, I became good at playing the guitar.

Some of my schoolmates invited me to join their band. At first, I was too shy to play in front of people. Then I realized that I enjoyed music more when I shared it with others. We had great fun playing music, and I made good friends with those in the band. Nowadays, our band is getting more and more popular. We often take part in performances both inside and outside our school.

Although I have become busier this year, I still love playing the guitar and manage to find time for it. Music makes me happy when I am feeling sad, and it relaxes me when I am stressed. It will always be part of my life.

title: Unit 1 · Chime-bells from the Tomb of Marquis Yi of the Zeng State
text:
In 1978, a set of chime-bells was unearthed from the tomb of Marquis Yi of the Zeng State in Suizhou, Hubei Province. These chime bells, crafted during the early Warring States Period, are now held as a precious treasure in the Hubei Provincial Museum. This amazing musical instrument consists of 65 bells of different sizes, arranged into three levels and eight groups. Among the set, the largest bell is as tall as 153.4 centimetres and as heavy as 203.6 kilograms.

The smallest one is only 20.4 centimetres tall and weighs 2.4 kilograms. Each bell produces two different, clear, and beautiful sounds.

The discovery of the chime-bell set surprised the world as it showed that the ancient Chinese had created such a musical instrument over 2,400 years ago. The instrument was played at important festivals and great celebrations in ancient times. It shows the musical development of ancient China.

title: Unit 1 · How does sport bring us together?
text:
The most recent was the 2022 Winter Olympics. A total of nearly 2,900 athletes attended and competed in 109 events in seven Olympic winter sports. There were many exciting moments. Nearly the whole world watched the fantastic figure skating and ski jumping competitions. I watched the freestyle skiing, and like everyone else, I fell in love with those brave and talented athletes. I also became a huge fan of the mascot, Bing Dwen Dwen.

And we shall not forget the amazing achievements in the 2008 Summer Olympics. I watched in wonder as Usain Bolt smiled his way across the finish line in the 100 metres, setting a new world record. Then I watched the drama of the shooting event. Du Li won her second Olympic gold medal, after the first one in 2004. Both were dramatic come-from-behind victories.

Hosting two Olympics brought challenges but also opportunities to Beijing. Both Games showed China's success in its reform and opening-up on the world stage. China's great achievements have gained worldwide attention. In both events, many volunteers and citizens helped out. They worked with pride to make sure that people from around the world had a pleasant stay.

Events like the Olympic Games build bridges between countries and form friendships between people. The purpose of the Olympics is to build relationships between people, to celebrate the Olympic spirit, and to bring people together for peace and harmony. This is shown in both the motto of the 2008 Olympics, "One World, One Dream", and the motto of the 2022 Olympics, "Together for a Shared Future". These mottos touch my heart quite deeply, as I'm sure they touch yours.

Junior high students need to take shot-put classes as part of their physical education.

Though he was defeated, he had competed to the best of his ability in the boxing match.

You may have never heard of my favourite athlete, Eric Moussambani, the first Olympic swimmer from Equatorial Guinea.

Eric swam in the 100-metre freestyle at the 2000 Sydney Olympics. However, he had just begun swimming only eight months before the Games! The only swimming pool for him was a hotel pool about 13 metres long, and even then he could only use it for an hour every morning. In fact, the first time he ever saw an Olympic-sized 50-metre swimming pool was at the Olympics.

During his race, he swam well for the first 50 metres, but the last 15 metres of the race were especially difficult for him. In fact, it looked like he was going to drown! But he tried hard and finished the race, winning loud cheers from the crowd.

Though Eric Moussambani is not an Olympic medal winner, he is still my favourite athlete. He never gave up no matter how hard it was. With hard work and practice, Eric later became quite fast at the 100 metres. His time for the 100-metre event improved from 1 minute 52 seconds, his Olympic record, to under 57 seconds! He later became the coach of the national swimming team for Equatorial Guinea, and he is a true example of the Olympic spirit.

title: Unit 1 · From Olympics to Mass Sports
text:
China hosted the Summer Olympics in 2008 and the Winter Olympics in 2022, both of which were successful. These sporting events have offered the world a deeper understanding of China and its people. Athletes, sports fans, and even ordinary citizens from other countries were amazed by China's rapid development, not only in sports but also in various fields.

has consistently paid attention to physical education and national health. During the 2022 Winter Olympics, more than 20% of the Chinese population actively joined in ice and snow sports. The Olympic motto "Faster, Higher, Stronger—Together" continues to supply a positive force to our society.

In addition to competitive sports, mass sports have gained popularity throughout China. Nowadays, one can easily see people of all ages participating in various outdoor activities such as rope skipping, running, guangchangwu, and roller skating. During the winter months, many families go skiing and mountain hiking to enjoy the fresh air. China is committed to providing greater convenience for people to join in physical activities during their free time. The goal is to have a public park or exercise trails near all residential communities.

title: Unit 1 · How do people celebrate festivals?
text:
Teng Fei: What's on your calendar next month, Clarice? Clarice: I'm going to Thailand to experience their New Year celebrations. Teng Fei: Wow, that will be fun, although I believe it's quite hot there. Clarice: Yes, that's true, but there's a water festival there from the 13th to 15th of April. Teng Fei: That must cool people down. Do you know you can also do the same in China? Clarice: Really? Where? Teng Fei: Well, there's also a water festival in Yunnan Province. Clarice: How exciting! I wonder if the two water festivals are similar. Teng Fei: Yes, they are. The Dai people's New Year celebration is usually in mid-April as well. People go into the streets and throw water at each other. Clarice: That sounds interesting. But why do they do that? Teng Fei: Well, according to their culture, the water washes away bad things. Then they'll have good luck in the new year. Clarice: I hope I'll get some good luck in Thailand!

Chinese people celebrate the Mid-Autumn Festival on the fifteenth day of the eighth lunar month. It is a time to reunite with family members. On that night, people admire the full moon and eat mooncakes. Mooncakes are traditional Chinese snacks in the shape of a full moon. They are symbols of reunion and show people's best wishes for the family and friends they love and miss.

There are many traditional stories about this festival. One is about Chang'e flying to the moon. In this story, a hero called Houyi received magic medicine as a gift. Anyone who took this medicine could live forever. Houyi planned to share it with his beautiful wife, whose name was Chang'e. However, a bad man tried to steal it, so Chang'e took all the medicine to protect it. Suddenly, she became very light, and she flew up to the moon! It is said that Chang'e has lived on the moon since then. How she wished to be reunited with her family again!

title: Unit 1 · What can festivals bring us?
text:
Chinese people consider the Spring Festival the most important. It is celebrated in January or February, and it is a time for everyone to say goodbye to the old year and give a warm welcome to the new one. There are lots of customs, such as sweeping out dust from houses, putting up couplets, setting off fireworks, and watching lion dances and dragon dances. One very important custom is for people to return home and reunite with their families. They especially enjoy the big family dinner on the eve of the Spring Festival. This is when grandparents, parents, and children come together to eat delicious food and express best wishes for the whole family.

In Egypt, people celebrate Sham El-Nessim in April to mark the beginning of spring. The name of the festival means "smelling the breeze". At this time, the weather becomes brighter, and the flowers and trees begin to show their colours. People paint eggs, which are symbols of new beginnings. They also go out to enjoy picnics, dance, sing, and watch plays at the theatre.

Although New Year celebrations are different throughout the world, something remains the same. In every country, it is a special time for people to spend time with their family and friends and show hope for the coming year.

How are you? I miss China, but I am happy to be back home in Brazil. It is February, so I am enjoying the Carnival in my hometown, Rio de Janeiro. This is my favourite festival. It is also one of the biggest carnivals in the world. During this time, we have hundreds of street parties all over the city.

The most important celebrations take place in the streets along the beach. You can see dance parades everywhere for days. A very traditional dance is the samba. Many dance schools in Rio prepare their own shows for the Carnival. We have a special place for these shows. It is like a huge stadium where the school groups can perform. Here you will hear people playing beautiful music and see them dancing in fantastic costumes.

This festival is so important for Brazil. It brings everyone together to celebrate the colourful culture and way of life here.

title: Unit 1 · Traditional Celebrations of the Longtaitou Festival
text: The Longtaitou Festival falls on the second day of the second lunar month each year. It holds significant importance in the Chinese cultural calendar, following the Chinese New Year and the Lantern Festival. In Chinese folk stories, the Chinese dragon is a legendary creature associated with rain. On this day, the Dragon King awakes from his winter sleep and raises his head. This event symbolizes the arrival of spring and the beginning of the farming season. As spring unfolds, insects and animals become more active, and the Among the traditional practices observed during the Longtaitou Festival, the most popular and widely practised one is getting a haircut. Many people believe that getting a haircut on this day can get rid of bad luck. As a result, barber shops are always busy during this festival, with customers often lining up for their turn. In addition, people also eat special food to celebrate the festival. In Fujian Province, people eat tofu balls to welcome good luck in both family life and business. Fried beans are the traditional food in parts of Shandong Province. Another traditional festival food, longxu noodles, is named after a part of the dragon's body in honour of this special day.

title: Unit 1 · How can we bring the past back to life?
text:
Among the many archaeological sites and museums throughout China, the Sanxingdui Museum in Guanghan, Sichuan Province, attracts millions of visitors from around the world every year.

Once visitors walk through the gates of the museum, they will be surprised by the amazing collection of cultural artefacts from the Bronze Age. The ancient people of Sanxingdui lived by the Yangtze River more than 3,000 years ago. However, people were not aware of them until the 20th century, when Sanxingdui was discovered. Thousands of gold, bronze, ivory, and jade objects were found underground.

The first big discoveries were in two pits in 1986. More than 1,000 artefacts were found and many were repaired, including the world-famous bronze tree, the huge mask, the bronze man, and the gold stick. More recently, in 2019, six more pits were found and dug in the area. More amazing artefacts were found in them, including some 3,000-year-old gold masks and bronze zun. By using modern technologies, researchers even found some remains of silk items. All the artefacts show that people from that era must have been highly skilled in metal work as well as carving. They might also have developed the skill of making silk.

The discovery of Sanxingdui amazed the world, and it has been called one of the world's greatest archaeological finds of the 20th century. It is especially mysterious as no writing has been found at the site, and the art style seems very different and unique. Historians think Sanxingdui gives important evidence for the study of the development of Chinese civilization.

For discoveries like Sanxingdui, it is never enough just to find the artefacts and their history. The Sanxingdui Museum has held exhibitions around the world. Visitors have all been amazed by these treasures. And now, with digital technology, the Sanxingdui Museum is looking for more ways to bring the past back to life. It aims to show more people these mysteries and to make young people more curious about history, the world, and more importantly, our human story.

Hello, everyone! I'd like to present to you a historical site from the Mayan civilization. Maybe you've heard about the Egyptian pyramids, but the Mayan people also built hundreds of pyramids throughout Central America from about 1,000 BCE to 1,500 CE. Here you can see the most famous example—the Pyramid of Kukulkan.

For the Mayans, Kukulkan was a snake god. Twice a year, when the day and night are in balance, the setting sun creates a strange shadow on one side of the pyramid. This shadow looks like the shape of a snake crawling down the steps. Interestingly, the building has a total of 365 steps. The Mayans could have built this to show the number of days in the solar year.

There's also another interesting fact about the pyramid. Inside there are two more pyramids. The Mayans must have built each pyramid on top of the other over a long period of time. Isn't that amazing?

So, from the Pyramid of Kukulkan, we can learn a lot about the ancient Mayan civilization. That's all! Thank you!

title: Unit 1 · History of Shandong Province
text:
Shandong Province is considered as one of the cradles of ancient Chinese culture. The fossil of the Yiyuan Ape Man is proof of primitive human beings as early as 600,000 years ago in Shandong Province. Beixin Culture, Dawenkou Culture, Longshan Culture, the defensive wall of the Qi State, and the Luozhuang Tombs of the Han Dynasty are all found in Shandong Province.

Shandong is the birthplace of a great number of historically famous figures who have brought great glory to the province. Confucius, Zengzi, Mencius, Zhuge Liang, Wang Xizhi, Li Qingzhao, Zhang Zeduan, Xin Qiji, and Pu Songling are all familiar to Chinese people.

the Qi State and the Lu State. The modern province of Shandong was formed during the Ming Dynasty. However, between 1898 and 1914, Jiaozhou Bay, part of Shandong Province fell under German control, with Qingdao serving as the administrative centre. China's support for the Allies during the First World War was aimed to regain Jiaozhou Bay from German control, but the Treaty of Versailles transferred the German-controlled region to Japan. This decision triggered strong dissatisfaction among the Chinese people, leading to the May 4th Movement. Finally, Jiaozhou Bay returned to China's control in 1922. At present, Shandong has become an important historical, cultural, and business centre in China.

title: Unit 1 · How can art inspire us?
text:
Last weekend, a friend and I went to visit an art museum. We found many works of traditional Chinese calligraphy on show. It was my first time to visit such an exhibition, and I was really excited. Although I don't know much about Chinese calligraphy, I can see it everywhere in China. It is in advertisements, on posters, and on buildings. Many homes have it on their walls or front doors. You may even come across people writing calligraphy with water and a big brush on the ground in a park. I came to learn that calligraphy is viewed by Chinese people as one of the highest forms of art.

In the museum, my Chinese friend told me an interesting story about calligraphy. Wang Xizhi (303-361) was one of the best calligraphers in history. He once attended a party at the Orchid Pavilion. Every guest was expected to write a poem during the party. At the end of the party, Wang wrote the introduction to the poems. The next day, Wang looked at his calligraphy—the Lanting Xu (introduction to the poems written at the Orchid Pavilion)—and realized that it was his best calligraphy ever. He then tried to reproduce the calligraphy in the exact same style, but found it impossible. When he was at the party, he was very happy and relaxed. This made his calligraphy especially lively. People later said that the calligraphy in the Lanting Xu looked like a Chinese dragon at play.

It is a pity that the original version of the Lanting Xu has been lost, but it was copied and studied by many calligraphers. In fact, calligraphy students today still copy the Lanting Xu, along with other famous works in history. Doing so not only helps them to improve their own calligraphy, but also develops their artistic senses.

While I still don't understand enough about Chinese calligraphy, I have begun to see the beauty in it beyond the meaning of the words. As an art form, it is meant to inspire, to make us think, and to show our understanding of beauty.

My favourite artist is Vincent van Gogh. He was born in the Netherlands in 1853. It was not until he was 27 that he decided to become a painter and began studying art. Van Gogh went to stay with his brother in Paris in 1886. There, he experienced the bright colours of famous French painters. This was when Van Gogh developed his famous style—using short brushstrokes of thick paint and bright colours. After moving to the countryside two years later, he painted his most famous works, including Sunflowers. With a painting like The Starry Night, we can see colours, imagination, and energy in Van Gogh's work. He was able to show the passion and feelings inside himself like few other people before or since. Sadly, he died in 1890.

I like Van Gogh because he showed passion and energy in his life. I like him also because he loved nature and painted it in all its beauty.

title: Unit 1 · Five Oxen
text:
Five Oxen is a painting by the famous artist Han Huang (723–787), who was born in Chang'an (the present-day Xi'an) in the Tang Dynasty. He was very skilful at painting animals, such as oxen and goats, with detailed facial expressions. At present, Five Oxen, 139.8 centimetres long and 20.8 centimetres wide, is kept in the Palace Museum in Beijing. In the painting, the five oxen are positioned in a line and have different appearances. Using simple but powerful lines, the painter sketched the oxen's bones, muscles, and hair on their heads.

In this painting, there is no background, and the colours are light and simple. Both their spirit and appearance are described perfectly. All the oxen have bright eyes that show their calm and resolute nature. It is said that the painting reflects the painter's stance. Throughout his life, Han Huang paid much attention to agricultural development, and this painting could be seen as an encouragement to the agricultural sector. Five Oxen is Han's only painting work that has been passed down to the present day and is one of the few Tang Dynasty paintings on paper. It has attracted much attention in the aspects of artistic achievement and historical value.

title: Unit 1 · What causes pollution?
text:
Host: T he problem of rubbish is becoming more and more serious nowadays. Dr Wu, what can we do about it? Dr Wu: Have you heard of the three Rs: reduce, reuse, and recycle? Host: Recycle! Everyone knows about that! We can recycle materials like glass, paper, plastic, and metal. Dr Wu: Yes, but while recycling is good, not everything can be recycled. The first thing we need to do is reduce our waste. Host: Could you tell us what we should do? Dr Wu: Well, you can buy products with less packaging. Also, buy only the food you need to reduce food waste. Host: And please tell us about the last R. Dr Wu: Sure. Reuse means using things again and again. Many things we use daily, like glass bottles and plastic bags, can be reused. We can also donate our clothes, books, and toys to people who need them. Host: Thank you, Dr Wu. I think we can solve the problem if everyone follows the three Rs!

Noise pollution can be caused by busy streets or loud machines. It can bother people so much that they suffer from hearing or memory loss. ...

title: Unit 1 · How can we protect our environment?
text:
Mr Chen was not a "Guardian of the River" before. He grew up on the banks of the Yangtze River and used to be a fisherman, like his father. Back then, parts of the river were smelly and yellow because of the waste from factories, restaurants, and homes. Fishermen were also catching too many fish. As a result, the number of fish and plants in the river was dropping quickly.

The government took action to deal with the problem before it was too late. New wastewater disposal centres were built to clean the wastewater before it went into the river. Laws were made to stop new factories from being built near the river. Boats were sent out to clean up the rubbish. Finally, fishing was banned in the Yangtze River for 10 years from 2020. Mr Chen and other fishermen were given new jobs as guardians to protect the river.

At first, Mr Chen was not used to working on the riverbank. Now he feels happy because he has a good job and a steady income. He is also glad to see that the Yangtze River has returned to what it used to be like when he was a child, with a lot of fish swimming in the clear water and beautiful birds enjoying their life on the bank. He is proud of his job. "Look there! That's my wife," Mr Chen said to the reporter. "She has joined a river clean-up team, and we work together to protect our mother river. We must protect it for our future generations."

We are deeply worried about the poor condition of our city's beach. The beach is no longer a nice place to spend time at because it is covered in waste. Broken glass stops us from walking on the soft sand. Birds and sea animals sometimes get trapped by plastic bags, or even worse, eat them as food. Part of the rubbish is washed up onto the beach by the sea. However, most of the litter is left by people who go there to enjoy themselves.

We need to take action before the problem gets worse. Teams from our school pick up rubbish on the beach every Saturday, but that is not enough. We hope that the city government will encourage more people to join our teams. Also, we need to set up more rubbish bins and make sure that people cooperate by throwing their litter in the bins before they leave. People should also try to bring their own bottles and bags so that there is less rubbish. I believe that we can solve this problem if we work together.

title: Unit 1 · Garbage Sorting Efforts
text:
Garbage sorting is everyone's responsibility to protect the environment and save natural resources. The concept of garbage sorting first came out in the 1950s. Residents in Beijing started sending items like newspapers, old clothes, and paper boxes to recycling stations to get money in return. By 2019, it had gained widespread recognition among the Chinese population. Garbage sorting is very important because it is good for soil, air, and water. For instance, plastic, wood, and paper can be recycled; fish bones, apple peels, and some plants can be transformed into organic fertilizer.

Shanghai led the way as the first city to carry out strict regulations about garbage sorting. Residents now face fines if they fail to sort their garbage correctly. The primary aim behind these fines is not to punish but rather to remind people of their environmental responsibilities. Besides Shanghai, more and more cities are also committed to educating their residents about the importance of garbage sorting, like Tianjin, Shenyang, Dalian, Jinan, and so on. To bring a bright future in environmental protection, we still have a long way to go.

title: Unit 1 · Where would you like to travel?
text: Guide: Look! Here's the Great Wall. Peter: Oh, it looks like a huge dragon! How long is it? Guide: That's a popular question. It is over 21,000 kilometres from east to west—that makes it the longest wall in the world. If we're only talking about the parts from the Ming Dynasty, it's about 8,850 kilometres long. Teng Fei: Is Badaling a part of the Ming Great Wall? Guide: Yes, it's the most famous part. Adam: Wow, amazing! When was the Great Wall built? Guide: It was first built in 770 BCE, and the ancient walls were later connected in the Qin Dynasty. Hundreds of thousands of people worked on the Great Wall. Adam: Unbelievable! What was the reason for building the Great Wall? Guide: The main reason was to protect the country in ancient times. Peter: What is the wall made of? Guide: It is made of stones, bricks, and other materials, and it's one of the Seven Wonders of the World. There are no other man-made objects as big as the Great Wall! Teng Fei: That's correct. We are proud of it.

title: Unit 1 · What can you learn from travelling?
text:
The well-known Confucius Temple, the Confucius Family Mansion, and the Cemetery of Confucius together are usually called "Sankong", a name for these three Confucius-related sites. Sankong enjoys great fame as a world cultural heritage site. A lot of tourists from China and abroad visit Sankong every year.

The Confucius Temple was built in the Zhou Dynasty. Because of some damage, it was not completed until the Ming and Qing dynasties. It was where people made offerings to Confucius. The temple takes up a large area, having nine large yards. In the temple, there are many trees that are over 500 years old.

The Confucius Family Mansion is the home of Confucius' following generations. It was built around 650 years ago. It covers a large area, having more than 400 rooms. In the Confucius Family Mansion, there is a study. This room was built in the Qing Dynasty. It shows that the Confucius family paid great attention to their children's education.

The Cemetery of Confucius is one of the greatest family tombs. Confucius was buried there, together with his family members and related members with the family name of Kong in different dynasties. The number of tombs now is over 100,000. The area is so large that most tourists have to take a bus to complete their tour of the Cemetery of Confucius.

The streets of Qufu are historical. Tourists can learn a lot about Confucius in Sankong. They will learn a lot about Confucius' life and thoughts. They will also gain a deep understanding of traditional Chinese culture.

I went to Suzhou, a cultural and historical city in Jiangsu Province, recently. I'd like to share something with you about my visit to Suzhou.

Suzhou is known around the world for its beautiful gardens. The history of the Classical Gardens of Suzhou can be dated back to the Spring and Autumn Period. According to the tour guide, the classical garden art of Suzhou was at its best during the Ming and Qing dynasties. Dozens of private gardens, such as Zhuozheng Yuan, Liu Yuan, Canglang Ting, and Shizilin, are still well-kept today. When I was in the different gardens, I could see each had their own features. They attract many tourists every year.

The Classical Gardens of Suzhou really represent the highest level of private garden design. When I was in the gardens, I felt like I was enjoying the designers' great art. There are many nice places for people to rest and relax, paths for people to walk along, and beautiful trees and flowers for people to enjoy.

In the gardens, I not only enjoyed seeing the old buildings, trees, stones, and ponds but also learned about the stories of the gardens. Walking through the gardens, I couldn't help thinking about the poems related to these gardens. Now I have a deeper understanding of those poems. I can feel the romance of the ancient people.

The Classical Gardens of Suzhou are really beautiful and I hope that I can go there again.

What will you take with you? (ID card, cell phone, suitcase, clothes, umbrella, some snacks... )

title: Unit 1 · The Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge
text:
The construction of the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge started on 15 December 2009. It cost a total of 126.9 billion yuan and took nine years to be completed. It was put into use on 24 October 2018. The Hong Kong-Zhuhai- Macao Bridge connects Hong Kong on the east bank of the Pearl River Delta to Zhuhai and Macao on the west bank. The bridge covers a distance of 55 kilometres, making it the longest sea-crossing bridge in the world. The project has set many world records. It provides valuable construction experience for building such sea-crossing bridges in the future. The bridge includes a tunnel that is 6.7 kilometres long—the world's deepest underwater tunnel.

A total of more than 400,000 tons of steel were used for the tunnel and the 22.9-kilometre bridge, which is enough to build 60 Eiffel Towers. The bridge was named one of the "seven wonders of the modern world".

The bridge was designed to withstand strong earthquakes and super typhoons. Before the construction of the bridge, it took more than 3 hours to drive from Hong Kong to Zhuhai and Macao. Now it takes only about 45 minutes. It is important not only to the development of bridge building but also to the economic and social development. The Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge is a testament to the collective efforts of thousands of individuals, reflecting the wisdom, strength, and determination of the Chinese people.

title: Unit 1 · What can be regarded as symbols of China?
text:
Li Na's vacation was terrible. Peter went to Weifang with Li Na. People from different countries compete in kite flying. Li Na saw many beautiful kites. Kites were only made of paper.

You look so beautiful! What kind of clothes are you wearing? Meimei: Hanfu, a kind of traditional clothing from ancient China. Oh, Hanfu has such a long history. Meimei: Yes, about thousands of years. It has changed greatly across different dynasties. When do people wear Hanfu now? Meimei: Teenagers are often seen wearing it at their graduation ceremonies or during holidays. Some people even wear Hanfu in their daily life. As a symbol of traditional Chinese culture, Hanfu is getting more and more popular with Chinese people. I've never worn it. What a pity! Meimei: Really? Hanfu shows are held every year. Hanfu can be seen everywhere. Why don't you try it on? Good idea! Clothing is a part of culture. It will help us know more about China. Meimei: Yes, I'm all for it.

title: Unit 1 · What do symbols tell us?
text:
China is the third largest country worldwide, next only to Russia and Canada. There are 56 ethnic groups in China. The official language of China is Standard Chinese. China has rich natural resources, colourful cultural heritage, and diverse customs.

China is an ancient country with great culture and about 5,000 years of history. The Spring Festival, an ancient festival, also enjoys thousands of years' history. Today, people still celebrate this traditional festival. They go back home to get together with their families every year during the festival.

China has lots of famous symbols, such as the Forbidden City, the Great Wall, the Five Great Mountains, pandas, peony, and so on. The Forbidden City in Beijing was the palace for 24 emperors throughout the Ming and Qing dynasties. The precious collections in it attract so many tourists. Pandas are the most popular animal in China. They are also one of the favourite animals among the Chinese people. The largest nature park for pandas is in Sichuan Province. The flower peony is regarded as the symbol of prosperity. It was much praised by the poets of the Tang Dynasty.

China also has many well-known lakes, such as Qinghai Lake, West Lake, Dongting Lake, and Poyang Lake. The Qinghai Lake is the largest saltwater lake in China. Among the rivers in China, the Yangtze River and the Yellow River are quite familiar to Chinese people. These two great rivers not only are popular, but also have special meanings. The Yangtze River, also known as the Golden Waterway, is the longest river in China. The Yellow River is called the Mother River by all Chinese people.

Did you know that tea, the second most popular drink in the world after water, was discovered by accident? Many people believe that tea was first drunk nearly 5,000 years ago. It is said that a Chinese chief called Shen Nong first discovered tea as a drink. One day Shen Nong was boiling water over an open fire. Some leaves from a tea plant fell into the water and remained there for some time. It produced a nice smell so he tasted the brown water. It was quite delicious. In this way, one of the world's favourite drinks was discovered.

More than 4,000 years later, Lu Yu, "the sage of tea", mentioned Shen Nong in his book Cha Jing. The book described how tea plants were grown and how to make tea. It also discussed where the finest tea leaves were produced and what kinds of water were used.

It is believed that tea was brought to Korea and Japan during the 6th and 7th centuries. In England, tea didn't appear until around 1660, but less than 100 years later, it had become the national drink. The tea trade from China to Western countries took place in the 19th century. This helped to spread the popularity of tea and the tea plant to more places around the world. So next time you have a cup of tea, think about its interesting long history.

title: Unit 1 · Lovely Grandpa Yuan Longping
text:
Yuan Longping was born on 7 September 1930, in Beijing. He is widely recognized as one of the most well-known agricultural scientists. From an early age, he was a hard-working student and often asked questions. Although his parents wanted him to have a job in medicine, Yuan Longping chose to study agriculture in Southwest Agriculture College in Chongqing. After graduating in 1953, he became a teacher. It was not until the 1960s that he shifted his focus to researching and improving rice production.

Yuan Longping worked in rice fields for many years, driven by his dream of ensuring that every Chinese person had enough rice to fill their bowls. However, his contributions went far beyond this aspiration. He overcame a lot of difficulties and developed the first hybrid rice variety in 1974. Over the next 50 years, Yuan Longping and his team continued their research, achieving a series of remarkable successes.

In addition, Yuan Longping and his team shared their knowledge with about 14,000 students from nearly 80 countries. His influence extended not only to China's agricultural development but also to global food security. He is remembered as a kind, strict, and diligent elderly figure. Sadly, our lovely grandpa passed away on 22 May 2021, at the age of 91. Although we lost the "Father of Hybrid Rice", his scientific spirit will last forever.

title: Unit 1 · What do you want to say upon graduation?
text:
Good morning, students, teachers, and guests. Welcome to our junior high graduation ceremony! To begin with, I would like to congratulate all the new graduates. You have worked a long time for this moment. I remember meeting you when you first came here, full of energy and curiosity. Today, I'm full of pride as I see a room filled with talented youths, full of hope for the future.

As you set out on your life's new journey, first, I would like to say, find your passion, and follow your dreams! Find what you really love, and put all your energy and effort into it. Turn your eyes to the stars and keep your feet on the ground.

Second, never give up! After graduation, everybody will be entering different schools. No matter where you go, you will face new challenges. See every challenge as an opportunity: an opportunity to grow, to learn, and to suc- ceed. So be brave and deal with your challenges through hard work. Always bear this in mind: Diligence leads to success in one's life. Hard work will not fail you.

Third, learn to be thankful. While you have worked hard to finish junior high school, you did not work alone. Many others have lent hands to help you, and they have worked equally hard to get you to this moment. These people—your parents, teachers, and friends—have helped make you who you are today. Always be thankful for their help. Cherish their love and care forever. Always remember who you are and where you came from.

Last but not least, the end of junior high is also the beginning of a new life. Give it your best shot, and have no regrets. I wish you all success, and I hope we will meet again one day!

Junior high school has been a great journey for me. I have learnt many things and gained not just knowledge and skills, but also friendship. The club activities have made my school life richer—many of you know how much I love our drama club! I will always treasure the unforgettable memories of my time here. And now, as hard as it is, it's time to say goodbye.

To our teachers, a big "Thank you!" for your hard work, guidance, patience, and support. To our parents and friends, I want to thank you from the bottom of my heart for your love and support. Together, we have gone through many ups and downs. All these experiences have helped us grow and prepared us for new challenges ahead.

Finally, to all my fellow graduating students, "Congratulations!" Just as our head teacher said at our graduation ceremony, let's follow our passions and keep working hard. Though our dreams may seem far away, they are worth fighting for.

title: Unit 1 · Gui Haichao: A Dream Chaser
text:
Gui Haichao, a fan of space exploration for many years, made his dream of travelling to space come true through his own efforts. In 1986, Gui Haichao was born in a small village in Yunnan Province. In 2003, he was excited and attracted by spacecrafts for the first time when he heard the news of the successful launch of the Shenzhou 5. In 2005, he went to university in Beijing to study spacecraft design and engineering, taking the first significant step toward his dream. In 2014, he graduated with a doctoral degree in spacecraft design. In 2017, he became a university professor and did a lot of scientific research on space.

Chances are always for those who are prepared. Gui Haichao loves long-distance running, biking, and swimming. This helped him build a strong body. In 2018, after rounds of physical checks and professional tests, he was selected as one of the chosen few from about 2,500 competitors for a space station project. On 30 May 2023, the Long March rocket set off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre in Gansu Province. Gui Haichao, who was only 37 years old, was one of the three crew members on the Shenzhou 16. He became the first Chinese civilian and scientist in space, and his story has set a good example for all young Chinese dream chasers.

title: Unit 1 · Young Inventors
text:
You may think that all inventors are adults with rich experience and university degrees, but you would be wrong. In fact, many famous inventions have been created by teenagers just like you.

At the age of three, Louis Braille became blind as a result of an accident. At a school for the blind, he was taught to read using books with raised letters. Blind people would run their fingers over the letters and guess their shapes. However, sometimes it was confusing because letters like "Q" and "O" were very similar, and they also took up too much space on a page. To solve these problems, a system was invented where letters were replaced with a code of raised dots. However, this new method was still too slow and difficult. At the age of 15, Braille made important improvements to the raised dot system. He made the code simpler and reduced the number of raised dots. Braille's system was incredibly successful and is still used today around the world.

Philo Farnsworth was a teenager when he read about the problem of creating an electronic television in a science magazine and became interested in it. One day, while he was working on a farm, he noticed the straight rows of crops, and it gave him an idea. Perhaps an image could be broken down into lines, changed into electronic signals, and then sent through the airwaves. For years, Farnsworth worked to develop his idea, but he faced many challenges along the way. Many people did not believe his idea would work, and he found it difficult to get money to pay for his research. However, he never gave up. When he was 21, he eventually succeeded in sending a simple image using his invention. This breakthrough was an important step in creating the modern televisions that we use for entertainment today.

These stories show that with a passion for solving problems, anyone can make a difference in the world, no matter how old they are. So, if you have an idea that you believe in, do not be afraid to go for it. Who knows? You may just be the next Louis Braille or Philo Farnsworth.

title: Unit 1 · All About Satellites
text: In October 1957, people listening to radios around the world heard something no one had ever heard before. For three weeks, there was just "beep, beep, beep". About one beep a second. Millions of people sat round their radios just listening for this beep. The beep itself was not all that amazing. The amazing thing was the place where it came from—space. The beep came from the world's first man-made satellite, Sputnik 1. Sputnik 1 was launched by the Soviet Union on 4 October, 1957. It was round, made of metal, and more than twice as wide as a basketball. It weighed about 84 kilograms, travelled at 29,000 kilometres an hour, and took 96.2 minutes to circle Earth. Sputnik 1 stopped beeping when its radio battery died on 26 October, and it burnt up when it fell back to Earth on 4 January, 1958. The launch of Sputnik 1 also began the age of satellites. The first satellites were used for research. Through them, we can better understand the world we live in. They also send back photographs that help us to make better maps of our world. Communication satellites were also soon developed. These allow TV and radio signals to be sent across oceans or to places thousands of kilometres away. This is how people can watch TV across continents and oceans. Weather satellites soon followed. These can tell us when a storm is coming or whether it will snow next week. One new kind of satellite that is now becoming more useful to the public is the positioning satellite. This satellite works with a highly complicated system, like the BDS (BeiDou Navigation Satellite System), which can tell us where our car or even our mobile phone is. It seems that there is no end to the possible uses of satellites. The only real limit to their use is our own imagination.

title: Unit 3 · The Beauty of Chinese Music
text: Last night, one of my Chinese friends took me to a traditional Chinese music concert. I have always wanted to see traditional Chinese music performed live. The most common Chinese instruments that I recognized were the erhu, pipa, guzheng, and dizi. The concert was a superb performance by Chinese artists, attended by both the elderly and the young. As a foreign audience member, I felt the legacy and continuation of traditional Chinese music in China, and I deeply felt the charm of traditional Chinese music. The first song that was performed was a familiar tune, "Molihua" ("Jasmine Flower"). It was one of the first Chinese folk songs to become popular outside of China. The romantic song, played in a simple five-note scale that is characteristic of Chinese music, expressed the love for natural beauty. It was adapted into the Italian opera Turandot by Puccini. It was also played during the 2008 Beijing Olympic Games, the opening ceremony of the 2010 Shanghai Expo, and the opening ceremony of the Youth Olympics in Nanjing in 2014. No wonder it sounded so familiar! My favourite performance was the erhu solo of "Erquan Yingyue". The piece has a poetic name, which means "Moon Reflected on Second Spring". The gifted performer was so expressive that I almost cried along with it as I listened. The piece is considered one of the masterpieces of Chinese string music and the most famous piece by Chinese musician Abing. Its sad beauty reminded me of the hardships in Abing's life, but under the sadness, I sensed the musician's optimism and deep love for life. The concert ended with "Chunjie Xuqu" (the "Spring Festival Overture"), the first movement of the Spring Festival Suite by Li Huanzhi. Composed in the 1950s, the piece was based on the folk music of northern Shaanxi. It depicts the Spring Festival celebrated in this region in China during the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression. The piece had a lively beginning, and then slowed down to a soothing tune. As the melody played, I felt as though I was among the crowd celebrating the Spring Festival in Shaanxi back then, sharing the people's uplifting spirit and their hopes for a bright future.

title: Unit 3 · The Paralympics—Strength and Spirit
text:
Every two years, millions of people from around the world turn on their TVs to watch the Summer or Winter Olympic Games. However, did you know that a few weeks later, the same city hosts another major sports event—the Paralympic Games?

The Paralympics is an international sports event for athletes with physical disabilities. The original idea came from a doctor named Ludwig Guttmann in England shortly after World War II. Guttmann was interested in improving the lives of soldiers dependent on wheelchairs. He therefore decided to arrange a sports competition between a small group of patients on the same day as the opening of the 1948 Olympic Games. This small event slowly grew, and in 1960 it became known as the first Paralympic Games. It was decided that from then on the Paralympics would be held in the same year and country as the Olympic Games. Nowadays, the Paralympic Games take place in the same cities as the Olympics and use the same venues a short time later.

At the beginning, the Paralympics were open only to people in wheelchairs. However, in 1976, athletes with visual and other physical disabilities were included. Generally, athletes at the Paralympics only compete against others with the same kind of disability.

The Paralympics' goal has always been to help those with disabilities to improve their physical health and bring them joy and purpose. The motto for the Olympic movement is "Faster, Higher, Stronger—Together". The Paralympic Games follow this motto, showing the amazing strength and spirit of athletes with physical disabilities.

title: Unit 3 · The 24 Solar Terms
text:
More than 2,000 years ago, the ancient Chinese developed the 24 solar terms—a unique "calendar" to understand nature. They divided the year into 24 periods, each lasting 15 or 16 days. These terms were a guide for farmers—informing them of when to carry out certain farming activities. Many traditional Chinese festivals and folk customs are also related to the 24 solar terms.

The year begins with lichun (Start of Spring). Among the many traditions for welcoming spring is a popular custom, "biting the spring", where people eat spring pancakes or spring rolls. As the temperature rises and rainfall increases, nature slowly awakens. Farmers prepare their fields so that they can plant their crops during guyu (Grain Rain), the last term of the season.

Lixia (Start of Summer) marks the transition from spring to summer. Summer is a busy time for farmers. During the third solar term of summer, mangzhong (Grain of Ear), farmers in northern China harvest winter wheat, while farmers in southern China are busy planting summer rice. "Ear"here means the top part of a grain plant, such as wheat, that contains the seeds. It is no wonder mangzhong sounds like "busy with planting" in Chinese!

Liqiu (Start of Autumn) marks the coming of a harvesting season. There is a saying that goes, "If it rains on the day of Start of Autumn, a good harvest is expected." By the day of qiufen (the Autumn Equinox), the middle point of autumn, the weather in most areas becomes cool and leaves change in colour from green to orange and yellow. The Mid-Autumn Festival, a festival full of poetry and imagination, is celebrated around this time. Families and friends gather to admire the full moon and eat mooncakes.

Winter is a time for farmers to store their harvests and rest. After lidong (Start of Winter), the weather gradually changes from cool to cold. A traditional custom on the day of Start of Winter is to eat dumplings. The delicious and nutritious dumplings embody a warm wish for a cozy winter. Dahan (Major Cold) is the final term of the year and the coldest time of the year. As the new year draws near, families start to prepare for the Spring Festival.

Today, the 24 solar terms still play an important role in life. They remind us of how nature changes through the year and reflect the Chinese wisdom of living in harmony with nature.

title: Unit 3 · Into the Unknown
text:
A lost city under the sea in the Atlantic Ocean. Gardens up in the air in an ancient city in the Middle East. These are just two famous examples of historical mysteries that have fascinated people for thousands of years. Why are people so interested in such things? Well, humans are naturally curious. We like to use our imagination. Even when reading, many people love to read about places and times that might not be possible to visit in real life. Also, we like to find explanations for the things we do not fully understand. Sometimes we may just want answers to the simple questions of where and why.

Around 360 BCE, the ancient Greek writer Plato told the story of Atlantis, an island in the Atlantic Ocean. The founders of the island were half god and half human, and they were very rich and powerful. However, when they became too greedy and wicked, the gods made a terrible night of fire and earthquakes, and the island sank into the sea.

Although it is probably just a legend, later European writers believed it could be true. There were many arguments as archaeologists tried to identify the actual location of the island. "Pick a spot on the map, and someone has said that Atlantis was there," said a professor at the New York State Museum. Some thought it could be in the Mediterranean Sea, while others said it might be off the coast of Spain. Yet another idea was that Atlantis could be Antarctica. But was the island real? We may never know.

Another famous mystery involves a wonderful collection of gardens in the ancient city of Babylon, south of today's Baghdad, the capital of Iraq. The Hanging Gardens of Babylon is one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Many writers described these gardens as having beautiful plants and flowers hanging from the walls of the city. However, unlike the other wonders, scientists today argue about whether these gardens ever existed at all. A researcher from Oxford University claimed that there were such gardens, but they could have been in a completely different city, Nineveh, which was near the modern city of Mosul, in northern Iraq. Unfortunately, both sites suffered damage from wars, so it may be difficult for archaeologists ever to solve this mystery.

title: Unit 3 · Rodin and Balzac
text:
One of the most famous modern sculptors is Auguste Rodin (1840–1917). Rodin was born in Paris, and he trained to be a sculptor from an early age. For many years, he had to make a living by decorating buildings.

work—The Age of Bronze—was completed that same year. It was so realistic that people thought he had just made a cast of a human body. When Rodin proved that it was truly his work, he became the talk of the town.

While The Thinker is Rodin's most famous sculpture, his sculpture of Balzac is also influential. Honoré de Balzac (1799–1850) was one of France's most beloved writers. After his death, it was decided in 1891 that a statue should be created in his honour. Rodin was supposed to complete the statue in 18 months, but in the end it took seven years! To make things worse, at first it was rejected by the public because people did not think it looked like Balzac at all. Rodin's reply was that the statue was not supposed to look like Balzac's body—it was supposed to show Balzac's character and spirit. Upset about the rejection, Rodin took the sculpture home and refused to show it again. It was not until 1939 that the first bronze version of the sculpture was created and put on display.

Today, the sculpture, Balzac, is celebrated as one of the first truly modern sculptures and as one of the greatest sculptures ever made. The importance of this work and others is that Rodin was able to break away from traditional Greek and Roman style sculptures and create something entirely new. Rodin's sculptures are full of emotion and life, and they speak to modern audiences in a way that traditional sculptures do not. This is why Rodin is still celebrated and studied by artists today.

title: Unit 3 · The Problem with Plastic
text:
Plastic is one of the most useful materials in the world. It provides many benefits to our lives because it is cheap and convenient. For example, two or three hundred years ago, clothes were quite expensive, so many people only had one or two sets of clothes to wear. Now, with plastics like nylon and polyester, clothes have become much cheaper. Plastic can also be used to replace other things that are rare or valuable. For example, things like piano keys, which were once made from ivory, are now usually made from plastic. This saved the lives of many elephants.

However, while plastic has many benefits, it also causes lots of problems. Some plastic is so strong that it takes more than 400 years to break down before returning safely to the environment. When plastic is put in a landfill, the harmful materials inside can get into the soil and water underground. When plastic rubbish is burnt, it fills the air with harmful gas. Another problem is that plastic rubbish is often thrown on the ground. Rain washes that rubbish into the rivers. From there, it is swept out to the sea. Sea animals can get caught in it or hurt by it. Worse yet, sometimes fish eat the plastic as food, and it gets into their bodies. When the fish get to our dining table, the plastic could get into humans' bodies and harm our health.

What can we do about these problems? The best solution, for now, is to use less plastic. For example, bring your own reusable bag when shopping. Buy products, such as clothing and toothbrushes, made of natural materials. Avoid buying products with plastic packaging. Say no to single-use plastic items—plastic spoons and forks, plastic food containers and straws, etc.

While plastic is convenient and useful, in the end, most of it will last longer on our planet than we will. Let us not leave this problem to our future generations when we can deal with it now.

title: Unit 3 · The Sydney Opera House
text:
The Sydney Opera House is one of the most famous buildings in the world. It is Sydney's best-known landmark and an international symbol. The Sydney Opera House is as representative of Australia as the Pyramids are of Egypt. The Opera House with a "sailing roof" was designed by the famous Danish architect, Jørn Utzon. The base for the building was started in 1959. Utzon spent four years designing the Opera House. In 1963, the designs were finished and the second stage of construction began. In 1967, the inside was decorated. It took 14 years in total to build the Opera House. In 1973, the Opera House was officially put into use.

The Sydney Opera House cost around 100 million dollars, which was funded by the public. It is about 183 metres long and 120 metres wide. The roof of the building consists of more than 2,000 panels. Each year, this fantastic building attracts over 200,000 tourists to visit or enjoy events in it.

The Opera House reaches out into the harbour. When seen from the air or a ferry, the skyline of the Sydney Opera House, the blue water of the harbour, and the Sydney Harbour Bridge are so beautiful, amazing, and unforgettable.

title: Unit 3 · Beijing Opera
text:
Beijing opera is a traditional form of Chinese drama, and it is the most popular Chinese opera genre. With a history of approximately 200 years, it developed from various other drama forms, primarily from "Anhui opera" which was popular in southern China during the 18th century.

Over the past centuries, the roles in Beijing opera have evolved and simplified into the four major roles we know today: Sheng, Dan, Jing, and Chou. The theatrical art form of Beijing opera includes singing, dancing, and spoken dialogue.

One foreign traveller described his initial experience of watching Beijing opera. He said, "I was somewhat bored at first, but gradually, I became more interested. Eventually, I was strongly drawn to Beijing opera, even though I knew nothing about the background of the drama."

Today, Beijing opera is considered one of China's cultural treasures and has also spread to other countries. It acts as a bridge, introducing traditional Chinese culture to other parts of the world.

title: Unit 3 · See It Through
text: When you're up against a trouble, If the worst is bound to happen, Meet it squarely, face to face; Spite of all that you can do, Lift your chin and set your shoulders, Running from it will not save you, Plant your feet and take a brace. See it through! When it's vain to try to dodge it, Do the best that you can do; Even hope may seem but futile, You may fail, but you may conquer, When with troubles you're beset, See it through! But remember you are facing Just what other men have met. Black may be the clouds about you You may fail, but fall still fighting; And your future may seem grim, Don't give up, whate'er you do; But don't let your nerve desert you; Eyes front, head high to the finish. Keep yourself in fighting trim. See it through!

title: Unit 3 · It's a Long Way
text:
It's a long way the sea-winds blow Over the sea-plains blue, — But longer far has my heart to go Before its dreams come true.

It's work we must, and love we must, And do the best we may, And take the hope of dreams in trust To keep us day by day.

It's a long way the sea-winds blow— But somewhere lies a shore— Thus down the tide of Time shall flow My dreams forevermore*.

Because of my fur and horns, many people have tried to hunt me before. That's horrible. You saved my life and I owe you. I won't let anyone know about you—I promise! You are a good man. I trust you. Goodbye! Thank you again, and goodbye! [The deer and the raven exit stage left. The man exits stage right.] Where is my servant? At your service, my king. Do you know anything about this nine-coloured deer? No, my king. Go find this deer right now! I will give a large reward to whoever finds it. Yes, my king!

[In the palace. The king and the queen sit. The guards and servants stand on the sides.] Come forward, good man. Do you really know where that deer is? If you can get the deer's fur and horns, I will give you the large reward I promised. Yes, my king. I will lead you to find that deer. [Scratches his face.] I'm terribly sorry. This man didn't keep his promise and did a terrible thing to you who saved his life. And all I thought about was what my wife wanted. I am so ashamed of myself. Will you please forgive me? You are a fine king. If you can just promise me one thing, I will forgive you. I will keep my word. Please tell me what it is. I hope your people can live with me in harmony from now on, instead of hunting me all the time. You have my word. It's so kind of you. It's time for me to leave. May you and your people live a good life. Goodbye! [Leaves the stage.] Goodbye! And thank you for your blessing! [Turns to the man.] I should have never trusted you. You betrayed the deer who saved your life. I'm a sinner. Have mercy on me, my king! I now order that no one should harm the nine-coloured deer. It will be protected and live a happy life unharmed by my people. And now, let's return to the palace! Yes, my king!

[At the ballroom in the palace. It is filled with people dressed in fine clothes and jewellery, talking, laughing, and dancing.] Thank you so much for bringing me to this ball! Look at the prince and the minister, and their wives. They look gorgeous with their dresses and their shiny diamonds. I'm so happy! As long as you're happy, my dear. Come and meet my boss. Mr Romponneau, this is my wife, Mathilde. Romponneau: [Walks up to Mathilde and bows.] Nice to meet you, madame. Your husband has been such a good help to me at work. And you look stunning tonight. May I have this dance? It's so nice to meet you too, Mr Romponneau. It's my pleasure. See you later, Loisel. Take your time and enjoy yourself. Look at that fair lady with her shiny diamond necklace. She looks gorgeous! Do you recognize her? No, I have never seen her at any ball. She must be a newcomer here, with a rich husband. Let me ask her for the next dance. Then we'll know more. [Mathilde dances with different people in turn. Loisel slowly falls asleep on a chair at the side of the room. After dancing for the whole night, Mathilde walks over to Loisel and wakes him up.] [Mathilde and Loisel look through all the jewellery shops in the city until they find a similar necklace.] Oh, look at this. It looks exactly the same as Jeanne's. We're so [In Loisel and Mathilde's new flat. It is much smaller and shabbier. Loisel comes back looking tired and stressed.] Hi dear, I'm so hungry. I went to the trade company after work and did the accounting there for three hours without dinner. I'm so sorry to hear that. Here's some soup. I made it with the last of our potatoes. After the day I've had, even potato soup is a feast for me. How was your day? It was just as terrible as every day has been. I washed all the dishes and clothes with cold water and my bare hands. I climbed up and down the four floors with buckets of water. I had the usual quarrel with Mrs Butcher because she wouldn't sell me cheese on credit. Well, look on the bright side! Next week, the loan for the necklace will finally be paid off, and we'll be free. We'll have our lives back again! But I'm no longer the beautiful young woman I once was. With all this hard work, I've aged 30 years! No, my dear. You're just too tired. Drink some hot soup and get some rest. Tomorrow will be another day. Thank you, my darling, but I can't. I have to go and do the laundry for that rich family up the hill. I'll be back late tonight. I have got two more cases of work. I didn't finish them last Sunday, so I can't walk with you there. Sorry. It doesn't matter. Give me your thick coat. It's getting cold outside. [Mathilde finishes her soup and leaves.] [One Sunday morning, Mathilde is walking slowly down a street. Jeanne walks towards her but does not recognize her.] Hello, Jeanne. Oh, madame. Do I know you? You must have the wrong person. It's me, Mathilde. Mathilde? Is that you? [Stares closely.] It really is you! How long has it been since we met last time? Ten years. Ten years? But look at you! Your hair is totally grey, and your hands are so rough. You must have been through a lot. What happened?
